title: How 5 NEW Starters Will DEFINE the 2026 Cleveland Browns Offensive Line Gamble
thumb_prompt: Five empty jerseys hanging in a dimly lit locker room with dramatic shadows, each jersey bearing a different number, positioned side by side against rustic metal lockers with dramatic overhead lighting creating a sense of complete transformation and uncertainty
thumb_subject: five offensive linemen in brown and orange jerseys standing shoulder to shoulder in silhouette, representing different builds from lean tackles to massive guards, seen from behind facing the field

paragraphs.text: Let me hit you with something absolutely wild. The Cleveland Browns are about to do something that might be unprecedented in NFL history. When they line up for Week One of the twenty twenty six season, they will likely have five brand new starting offensive linemen. Five. Not one. Not two. All five positions from left tackle to right tackle could feature players who were not on the roster last year. Think about that for a second. This is not a rebuild. This is a complete demolition and reconstruction of the foundation of your football team.

To understand how massive this is, you need to know what Cleveland is walking away from. Joel Bitonio. Wyatt Teller. Jack Conklin. Ethan Pocic. These were not just players. These were Browns stalwarts. Bitonio made four consecutive Pro Bowls. Teller was Second Team All Pro in twenty twenty and twenty twenty one. Conklin was First Team All Pro in twenty twenty. In twenty twenty three, Pro Football Focus ranked this offensive line third in the entire league. This was elite talent. Championship caliber talent. And the Browns let every single one of them walk away.

Now here is the brutal truth. The Browns had to do this. That elite offensive line from twenty twenty three became one of the worst units in football in twenty twenty five. Injuries decimated them. Age caught up with them. They went from top ten to bottom five in a single season. Bitonio, Pocic, Teller, and Conklin all had contracts expiring. Dawand Jones, the one potential returning starter, suffered a season ending injury in Week Three and is still recovering. Cleveland had no choice but to blow it up and start over. But choosing to rebuild and successfully rebuilding are two very different things.
card_lines: Top 10 to bottom 5 in one year

paragraphs.text: This connects to a painful pattern in Browns history. Remember the Joe Thomas era? For eleven seasons, Thomas was the rock. A ten time Pro Bowler. A Hall of Famer. He anchored that left tackle spot from two thousand seven to twenty seventeen. The Browns tried for years to build around him and could never quite get it done. When Thomas retired, there was a void. Bitonio tried to carry that torch. He played twelve seasons in Cleveland. He was the longest tenured Brown before he retired this past June. And now he is gone too. These transitions hurt. Losing franchise cornerstones always does.

So who are the replacements? Let me walk you through what Andrew Berry did this offseason. He attacked every avenue possible. Free agency. Trades. The draft. The Browns traded for right tackle Tytus Howard from Houston. They signed center slash guard Elgton Jenkins and guard Zion Johnson in free agency. They re-signed guard Teven Jenkins. Then in the draft, they went all in. First round, ninth overall pick: Spencer Fano, offensive tackle from Utah. Third round, eighty sixth overall: Austin Barber, offensive tackle from Florida. Fifth round: Parker Brailsford, center from Alabama. Three draft picks on offensive line. This was the priority.

Spencer Fano is the crown jewel. The Outland Trophy winner. Unanimous All American in twenty twenty five. Pro Football Focus gave him a ninety three point zero grade last season, the best among all FBS tackles. His run blocking grade of ninety three point six was the best in the country by over three points. This kid played right tackle at Utah but Cleveland is flipping him to the left side to protect the blind side. That is a massive ask for a rookie. You are taking the ninth overall pick and immediately putting him in the most important position on your offensive line. High risk. High reward.
card_lines: Switching RT to LT as rookie

paragraphs.text: Austin Barber is the wildcard. Cleveland traded up to get him. They gave up picks one zero five, one forty five, and two zero six to the Chargers to jump up to pick eighty six. Why? Because Barber has elite athleticism. He scored a nine point eight four out of ten on the Relative Athletic Score. Six foot seven, three hundred twenty pounds, and he ran fast and jumped high at the combine. He allowed just three sacks in thirteen starts at left tackle for Florida last year. The Browns are moving him to right tackle. So both rookie tackles are switching sides. That is a coaching challenge for new offensive line coach George Warhop.
card_lines: Traded up from 105 to 86 to get him

paragraphs.text: The veterans they signed are question marks. Tytus Howard has talent but he has had injury issues. Zion Johnson was a bust in San Diego. Elgton Jenkins had a big injury last year. Teven Jenkins has had struggles. An offensive line is only as good as its weakest link. And right now, all five starters have legitimate reasons to be concerned about whether they could be that weak link. This is not a proven unit. This is a hope and a prayer that versatility, youth, and coaching can gel into something functional by September.

Head coach Todd Monken acknowledged the challenge on Day Ten of training camp. He said they are still trying to find the best five. Working through combinations. Fitting talent together. As of Day Twelve, reported by Dawgs By Nature, Elgton Jenkins has been exclusively at center and Tytus Howard has stuck to right tackle. Monken said right guard is the only spot still in competition and veteran Teven Jenkins has the upper hand. So the projected starting five looks like this: Spencer Fano at left tackle, Zion Johnson at left guard, Elgton Jenkins at center, Teven Jenkins at right guard, and Tytus Howard at right tackle. That is your line. Five new faces.

Behind those starters, things get interesting. Dawand Jones is back from that LCL tear and hamstring avulsion he suffered in Week Three last year. He participated in OTAs and minicamp. He has been getting reps with both the first and second teams as the coaches evaluate his progress. If Jones can get healthy and stay healthy, he provides crucial swing tackle depth. But that is a massive if. Injuries have plagued his young career. The Browns need him because if either Fano or Howard goes down, the backup plan gets shaky fast.

Austin Barber could also be that swing tackle. In fact, on Day Twelve of camp, Barber was at left tackle with the second unit while Dawand Jones was at right tackle. The Browns are cross training these guys for versatility. That is the common thread Andrew Berry prioritized. Players who can play multiple positions. Because in the NFL, you will have injuries. You will have guys banged up. If your backups can only play one spot, you are in trouble. Cleveland is trying to build a unit where guys can shift around and fill holes. It is smart. But it only works if the talent level is high enough.

Parker Brailsford, that fifth round center from Alabama, is also in the mix. He was getting first team reps in early practices according to reports. The coaching staff is giving him a real shot to push for playing time. That is what you want to see. Rookies competing. Dawand Jones, KT Leveston, and Barber are all battling for backup tackle roles. At guard and center, you have backups trying to prove they belong on the fifty three man roster. This is training camp at its core. Competition. Every rep matters. Every practice is an audition.
card_lines: Jones, Leveston, Barber for backup T
Guard/center backups fighting for roster spots

paragraphs.text: Compare this to the continuity Cleveland used to have. In twenty twenty two, the Browns had Jedrick Wills, Joel Bitonio, Ethan Pocic, Wyatt Teller, and Jack Conklin. Four of those five guys played together for multiple years. They knew each other's tendencies. They communicated without thinking. That chemistry is what makes offensive lines elite. You cannot just plug in five new guys and expect them to play like they have been together for years. The timing. The calls. The adjustments. All of that takes reps. And the Browns do not have the luxury of a full offseason. They have training camp and three preseason games to figure it out.
card_lines: 2022 line: 4 of 5 played together for years
Limited time to gel before Week 1

paragraphs.text: Let me put this in perspective. Has an NFL team ever started five completely new offensive linemen from Week One of one season to Week One of the next? I am not sure anyone has done the research, but it seems incredibly rare. Maybe unprecedented. The offensive line is the one position group where continuity matters more than anywhere else on the field. You need those five guys working as one unit. Five new starters means five guys learning each other on the fly. That is terrifying. Especially when you consider Cleveland's quarterback situation is also unsettled. Deshaun Watson or Shedeur Sanders will be back there. And they need protection.
card_lines: 5 new starters from year to year?
Possibly never done in NFL history
OL needs continuity more than any position

paragraphs.text: The good news? Todd Monken knows offensive line play. He has been around the game for decades. His time as Baltimore's offensive coordinator showed he can scheme around his personnel. George Warhop, the new offensive line coach, has a long track record in the NFL. These are not inexperienced coaches throwing darts at a board. They have a plan. The question is whether the talent can execute that plan. Spencer Fano has elite traits. Austin Barber has upside. The veterans have experience. On paper, this could work. But paper does not play football. Pads do.
card_lines: Plan exists, execution is the question

paragraphs.text: There is another layer to this story. The Browns revamped their offensive line at the same time they lost Myles Garrett on defense. They traded the two time Defensive Player of the Year to the Rams for Jared Verse and draft picks. That was a massive move. So Cleveland is rebuilding on both sides of the ball. Offense and defense. The offensive line overhaul and the post Garrett era are happening simultaneously. This is a franchise in transition. Todd Monken, the new head coach, is inheriting a team in flux. Young. Unproven. High upside but low floor. It is all or nothing.
card_lines: Lost Myles Garrett to Rams trade
Rebuilding OL and defense at once
Monken: new HC, team in flux

paragraphs.text: Here is what I am watching. Can Spencer Fano handle left tackle as a rookie? That is question number one. If he struggles, this entire offense could collapse. Question two: can the interior trio of Zion Johnson, Elgton Jenkins, and Teven Jenkins hold up in the run game? Cleveland needs to be able to run the football. Question three: how long does it take for these five guys to gel? If it takes six weeks, the Browns could be one and five before they figure it out. If it takes two weeks, they might steal a few early wins and build confidence. Timing is everything.
card_lines: Can Fano handle LT as a rookie?
Can interior trio hold up in run game?
How long to gel as a unit?

paragraphs.text: The last piece is this. Joel Bitonio personified consistency for twelve years. He set a standard. He showed what a Browns offensive lineman could be. Same with Joe Thomas before him. These guys were pillars. Legends. Now Spencer Fano, Austin Barber, and Parker Brailsford are walking into that legacy. They are the new generation. And they have enormous shoes to fill. If Fano can become a Pro Bowl tackle, if Barber can develop into a ten year starter, if this group can build its own identity and sustain excellence for years, then the Browns will have successfully transitioned from one era to the next. That is the dream. The reality? We will find out starting Week One.
card_lines: Joe Thomas: Hall of Fame pillar
Can they build their own dynasty?

paragraphs.text: So yeah. Five new starters. An unprecedented offensive line overhaul. A gamble that could define the Cleveland Browns twenty twenty six season and beyond. Andrew Berry went all in. Todd Monken and George Warhop have to make it work. Spencer Fano has to be the franchise left tackle from Day One. And this unit has to come together fast because the season starts in three weeks. No continuity. No chemistry. Just hope, talent, and a lot of reps in training camp. This is the story nobody is talking about enough. But it might be the most important storyline for the entire Browns season. Buckle up, Dawg Pound. This is going to be fascinating to watch.
card_lines: Berry all in, Monken must execute
